page-open-source-meta-description: Free and open source software puts control back with the people who use it. Learn what open source means, what it makes possible, and why Ethereum is built in the open.
page-open-source-hero-description-1: So much of daily life depends on software, from the phone in your pocket, the services in your home, to the apps you use every day. When a single platform controls those tools, it gains unhealthy power and dictates how you're allowed to use them.
page-open-source-hero-description-2: Free and open source software puts that power back where it belongs: with the user, ensuring technology serves you and your community over corporate interests.
page-open-source-summary-item-1: Open source means that the underlying technology is publicly available for anyone to use, copy, improve, or build on.
page-open-source-summary-item-2: Modern digital life trades your sovereignty for convenience. Free and open source software is the practical path back, giving you privacy and protection from monetary exploitation.
page-open-source-summary-item-3: You don't need to read code to benefit. Openness means independent experts can check what software really does, and their scrutiny protects everyone.
page-open-source-summary-item-4: Ethereum is built in the open. Its specifications, client software, and even this website can be inspected and improved by anyone.
page-open-source-ownership-title: When the things you buy stop being yours
page-open-source-ownership-description-1: Most of your digital life is operated by a handful of big companies. You may not be able to see how your data is used, why your feed algorithm changes, and have no recourse when a feature you rely on disappears. In exchange, everything is convenient.
page-open-source-ownership-description-3: In 2009, Amazon reached into customers' Kindles and remotely deleted books people had bought and paid for.
As recently as 2024, Spotify discontinued its Car Thing device and remotely disabled units that customers had purchased.
page-open-source-ownership-description-4: These cases show the risk of closed software: when a product depends on code and servers controlled by one vendor, that vendor can decide whether the product continues to work.
page-open-source-ownership-description-5: Open source changes the balance. When the code behind a product is public and its license grants meaningful rights, people can inspect it, run it, repair it, adapt it, and continue it independently. It is the same argument the right-to-repair movement makes about hardware, applied to the software inside it.
page-open-source-definition-title: What does "free and open source" mean?
page-open-source-definition-description-: Free/libre and open source software (FLOSS, also written FOSS) is software whose source code is public for anyone to run, study, share, and improve. Think of a dish that comes with its full recipe: you can check the ingredients, cook it yourself, pass it on, or make it better. Closed software keeps the recipe and ingredients secret, so one company decides what goes in, who may eat, and whether you ever find out.
page-open-source-definition-examples-lea: You have almost certainly used open source software today without noticing:
page-open-source-definition-example-linu: Linux, the base of every Android phone and most of the servers behind the websites you visit.
page-open-source-definition-example-fire: Firefox, one of the few major browsers with an independent engine of its own.
page-open-source-definition-example-sign: Signal, a messaging app whose encryption protocol also secures every WhatsApp message.
page-open-source-definition-example-vlc: VLC, the media player that opens the file nothing else will.
page-open-source-definition-example-libr: LibreOffice, a full office suite that reads the documents you already have.
page-open-source-definition-description-: "Free" here means freedom, not price. A program can cost money and still be free software; a no-cost app can still be closed and restrictive.

The idea is simple: if a company controls the code, the company controls the user. Free software flips that. It guarantees, legally and permanently, that the software answers to you. In plain language, it grants four freedoms:
page-open-source-freedom-run-description: Run the program as you wish, for any purpose, on your own terms.
page-open-source-freedom-study-descripti: Examine the source code to see exactly how the program works, then change it to suit your own needs.
page-open-source-freedom-share-descripti: Give other people exact copies of the program, so they can use it too.
page-open-source-freedom-distribute-desc: Release your modified version, so the wider community benefits from your changes.
page-open-source-possible-description: Free software is a neutral, universally accessible tool for controlling your own digital life. It belongs to no political ideology or movement, and it works the same for everyone who runs it.
page-open-source-benefit-trust-descripti: Open code lets independent people inspect how software works. Security, privacy, and accessibility claims can be tested rather than accepted on faith.
page-open-source-benefit-leave-descripti: Open software and open formats can make it easier to move your data and avoid being locked into one vendor (the details still matter, as open products should also provide practical export and migration options).
page-open-source-benefit-outlives-descri: When a company shuts down or moves on, open code lets anyone keep the lights on.
page-open-source-collaboration-descripti: Open source allows people to learn from one another's work, report bugs, translate text and images, write documentation, improve accessibility, and build tools for individual needs that a commercial roadmap might overlook.
page-open-source-repair-description: A device usually dies when its software does. Updates stop, the server goes dark, and working hardware becomes waste. The right-to-repair movement fights this in law by requiring that hardware you purchase can be repaired if it breaks; open source is the software half of the same fight. When the code can be read and rebuilt by anyone who owns the device, it outlasts its developer's interest in selling you the next version.
page-open-source-speech-description: Publishing code is speech, and it has had to be defended as such. The right to publish encryption software was won in court in the 1990s. The reverse holds too. When one company controls a tool, it decides what can be said, read, or built with it. Software anyone may copy and republish cannot be quietly switched off.
page-open-source-fork-description: If maintainers take a project in a bad direction, the community can copy the code and continue on their own path. Popular tools like LibreOffice, Jenkins, and OpenTofu all exist because communities exercised this right when corporate owners changed course. Forks are the safeguard against capture.
page-open-source-history-title: The long arc of software freedom
page-open-source-history-description-1: Software went from a bundled giveaway, to a product you bought, to a commons anyone could fork, to a subscription that watches you. The way you pay changed with it, and so did what was actually being sold.
page-open-source-history-description-2: Each card is one era. Open it to step through what happened, how you paid, and what you were really buying. Finish a chapter and it hands you the next.
page-open-source-history-start-hint: Each chapter also stands on its own, so you can start anywhere.
page-open-source-history-ledger-pay: How you paid, era by era
page-open-source-history-ledger-sold: What was sold, era by era
page-open-source-history-c1-hook: Code shipped free with the machine, until IBM put a price tag on it.
page-open-source-history-c1-s1-headline: Software used to be the free part.
page-open-source-history-c1-s1-body: Computers were leased by the month, and the programs came with them. Source code often traveled with the install, because sites had to patch it locally. Almost nobody thought of software as a product in its own right.
page-open-source-history-c1-s2-headline: June 1969: IBM puts a price on code.
page-open-source-history-c1-s2-body: Facing a federal antitrust suit, IBM unbundles. From 1970 its application programs carry their own monthly charge, separate from the machine. Software becomes a product with its own price tag, and an independent software industry finally has room to grow.
page-open-source-history-c1-s3-headline: Sharing was simply how it worked.
page-open-source-history-c1-s3-body: User groups like SHARE (1955) and DECUS (1961) traded source tapes freely. AT&T, barred from selling software by a 1956 antitrust settlement, licensed Unix with full source to universities for a nominal fee. A generation learned on readable code.
page-open-source-history-c1-s4-body: IBM leased its machines by the month, and after unbundling its application software was billed the same way, for as long as you used it. The subscription is not a modern invention. It is where the industry started.
page-open-source-history-c1-s4-stat-deta: Monthly lease, software included, then a monthly charge of its own.
page-open-source-history-c1-s5-body: Software was a sweetener, then a line item. What you paid for was the computer, and a vendor who answered the phone when it broke.
page-open-source-history-c1-s6-body: Once code has a price, someone will want to stop you from copying it. Next: what happens when the source stops shipping.
page-open-source-history-c2-hook: Source disappears behind license agreements. Stallman answers with a license that cannot be closed.
page-open-source-history-c2-s1-body: Personal computers put software in a box on a shelf, sold to millions who would never see the code. In 1980 the United States confirmed that software is copyrightable, and a 1983 court ruling extended that to machine code. Copies can now be made legally scarce.
page-open-source-history-c2-s2-body: In 1983 IBM stops shipping source. In 1984 AT&T, freed by its breakup to sell Unix, prices a commercial source license at $43,000. Shrink-wrap agreements arrive: you own the disk, but the terms say you only license what is on it. No reading it, no fixing it, no lending it.
page-open-source-history-c2-s3-headline: A license that cannot be closed.
page-open-source-history-c2-s3-body: In 1983 Richard Stallman announces GNU, and in 1985 the Free Software Foundation. The GPL (1989) turns copyright inside out: take the code, change it, share it, but pass the same freedoms on. In August 1991 Linus Torvalds, a Finnish student, announces a free operating system kernel, "just a hobby." Linux.
page-open-source-history-c2-s4-headline: Buy the box, own the copy.
page-open-source-history-c2-s4-body: For the first time, ordinary people paid for software once and kept it. One payment, a disk, a manual, and a license that lasted forever. Upgrades cost extra, but nobody could take away the version you had.
page-open-source-history-c2-s4-stat-deta: Boxed software, perpetual license, paid upgrades.
page-open-source-history-c2-s5-body: A copy costs almost nothing to make. The license, not the economics, is what keeps it rare, and the customer's leverage after the sale drops to zero.
page-open-source-history-c2-s5-stat-deta: Scarcity manufactured by license, not by cost.
page-open-source-history-c2-s6-headline: Now there are two ways to make software.
page-open-source-history-c2-s6-body: One keeps the code secret and sells copies. The other publishes it and invites you to copy. Next: can anyone make a living from the second?
page-open-source-history-c3-hook: Linux, Apache, and the open web. Red Hat proves free code can carry a business.
page-open-source-history-c3-s1-headline: Free code quietly takes over the plumbing.
page-open-source-history-c3-s1-body: By the late 1990s Apache serves most of the web. BIND resolves its names, Sendmail moves its email, OpenSSL encrypts its traffic. The internet itself runs on code anyone can read, written largely by volunteers and university researchers.
page-open-source-history-c3-s2-headline: Own the stack, lock the door.
page-open-source-history-c3-s2-body: Microsoft dominates the desktop and guards it with closed file formats and closed protocols: change the format, and everyone has to upgrade. Antitrust cases follow in the United States (1998) and Europe, which in 2004 orders Microsoft to share interoperability information. Also in 1998, the DMCA makes breaking a digital lock illegal, even on something you own.
page-open-source-history-c3-s3-headline: "Open source" gets a name, and a business model.
page-open-source-history-c3-s3-body: In 1998 Netscape publishes its browser source and the term "open source" is coined, a business-friendly framing of the same freedoms. In 1999 Red Hat goes public. The code stays free; customers pay for support, certification, and someone accountable.
page-open-source-history-c3-s4-headline: The code is free. Accountability is not.
page-open-source-history-c3-s4-body: Red Hat's bet: companies will pay yearly for a tested build, security updates, and a phone number, even when the same code is free next door. They did.
page-open-source-history-c3-s4-stat-deta: Free code, paid subscription for support and assurance.
page-open-source-history-c3-s5-body: When the code is shared, every fix is fixed for everyone. What you buy is confidence that someone is watching, and the hours you did not spend doing it yourself.
page-open-source-history-c3-s5-stat-deta: Nobody pays twice to fix the same bug.
page-open-source-history-c3-s6-headline: The commons is load-bearing, and it pays.
page-open-source-history-c3-s6-body: Free software now runs the internet and supports real companies. Next: what happens when everyone else builds on top of it.
page-open-source-history-c4-hook: Everything is built on open source. Almost nothing you buy is.
page-open-source-history-c4-s1-headline: Open source wins the foundation, and loses you.
page-open-source-history-c4-s1-body: Your phone, your cloud, your apps: nearly all of it runs on open code underneath. But the part you touch, the account, the app store, the service, is closed. Open source became infrastructure, and infrastructure is invisible.
page-open-source-history-c4-s2-body: App stores (2008) put a gatekeeper and a 30 percent toll between you and most programs on your phone. Adobe retires the perpetual Creative Suite for Creative Cloud (2013), and Microsoft steers Office toward the Office 365 subscription (2011). Stop paying, and the software you made your files with stops letting you edit them. "Free" apps are funded by ads instead.
page-open-source-history-c4-s3-headline: The right to fork gets exercised.
page-open-source-history-c4-s3-body: GitHub (2008) makes contributing ordinary. The AGPL (2007) gives projects a license that closes the loophole that let web services run free code without sharing their changes. And when Oracle moves to buy Sun (2009-2010), communities fork: MariaDB, LibreOffice, and Jenkins exist because people walked away with the code.
page-open-source-history-c4-s4-body: The subscription IBM pioneered comes back, now for photo editors and word processors. Your files remain yours. The program that opens them does not.
page-open-source-history-c4-s5-body: You no longer receive a thing. You receive permission, renewed monthly, revocable at any time. On the free tier the product is your attention, auctioned to advertisers.
page-open-source-history-c4-s5-stat-deta: And on the free tier, your attention.
page-open-source-history-c4-s6-body: The open stack underneath keeps working. The closed layer on top keeps the relationship. Next: what happens when renting is not enough for them.
page-open-source-history-c5-title: Re-enclosure, and you as the product
page-open-source-history-c5-hook: Licenses retreat, forks answer, and your data becomes the invoice.
page-open-source-history-c5-s1-headline: The bill comes due in two directions.
page-open-source-history-c5-s1-body: Consumers learn what "free" cost: the Cambridge Analytica revelations (2018) show how far behavioral data travels. Meanwhile companies built on open source start pulling the code back behind restrictive licenses. Both are the same move: lock the exit.
page-open-source-history-c5-s2-body: Telemetry is on by default and feeds are tuned for engagement. Broadcom buys VMware (2023) and ends perpetual licenses, forcing existing customers onto subscriptions. MongoDB (2018), Elastic (2021), HashiCorp (2023), and Redis (2024) swap open licenses for restrictive ones, mid-stream, after years of community contributions.
page-open-source-history-c5-s3-body: Elastic, HashiCorp, and Redis are each answered by a fork within weeks to months: OpenSearch, OpenTofu, Valkey. The forkers were often rival vendors protecting their own hosted products, not volunteers. Still, with a way out in place, Elastic adds an open license back in 2024, and Redis follows in 2025.
page-open-source-history-c5-s4-body: Per seat, per month, per use, per AI feature, priced to what it would cost you to leave. On the "free" tier you pay in data: location, contacts, habits, harvested as you go.
page-open-source-history-c5-s4-stat-deta: Seats, metered usage, AI add-ons, and your data.
page-open-source-history-c5-s5-body: An old line, from 1973 television criticism and a 2010 internet forum: if you are not paying, you are the product. Now you pay, and you are still the product. The surveillance stayed when the subscription arrived.
page-open-source-history-c5-s5-stat-deta: Rent for access, data harvested en route.
page-open-source-history-c5-s6-body: Complaints rarely changed the terms. Regulation moves one market at a time and makes the model visible, not obsolete. What worked fastest was the right to take the code and leave. Next: what that means for what you install tomorrow.
page-open-source-history-c6-title: So what do we do about it?
page-open-source-history-c6-hook: The case for choosing, and funding, the open counterpart.
page-open-source-history-c6-s1-headline: Almost every closed product stands on an open one.
page-open-source-history-c6-s1-body: The servers, databases, and libraries under almost every subscription are free software. The difference between the two layers is not quality. It is who holds the exit. With open code you can leave, and because you can leave, you rarely have to.
page-open-source-history-c6-s2-headline: Free is the license, not the cost.
page-open-source-history-c6-s2-body: A 2024 Harvard study estimated that widely used open source would cost about $4 billion to write once, but $8.8 trillion if every firm had to replace it, with 96 percent of that value coming from 5 percent of developers. Log4Shell (2021) and the xz backdoor (2024) show how much rests on so few people.
page-open-source-history-c6-s3-headline: Own the stack you are still allowed to own.
page-open-source-history-c6-s3-body: Pick the open counterpart where it is good enough, and file the bug where it is not. Pay maintainers what you would have paid a vendor. Prefer open formats, so leaving stays cheap. Using free software costs almost nothing. Sustaining it is the price of not repeating the last seventy years.
page-open-source-switch-title: How to switch to open source apps
page-open-source-switch-description-1: You do not need to replace everything at once. Start with one tool you use often, and explore whether any widely-adopted open source alternatives for that tool exist. Different open source alternatives may be optimized for the outcomes that matter most to you, like better privacy, fewer subscriptions, local control, data portability, or the ability to contribute.
page-open-source-switch-description-2: Consider tradeoffs honestly before making a full switch. FLOSS and privacy-protecting software sometimes trade convenience for control. Anti-tracking protection may occasionally break heavily scripted websites, untracked search may lack hyper-localized predictions, and maps that refuse to follow you may lack real-time traffic data. You can download and try an open source alternative to see if it meets your needs before fully migrating off of a closed app.
page-open-source-app-bitwarden-descripti: A password manager that syncs across all your devices
page-open-source-app-brave-description: A familiar browser that blocks trackers by default
page-open-source-app-firefox-description: An independent browser built by a non-profit, not based on Chromium
page-open-source-app-signal-description: A mainstream chat app with gold-standard encryption
page-open-source-app-cryptomator-descrip: Encrypts your files before they reach the cloud
page-open-source-app-thunderbird-descrip: A long-standing desktop mail client that works with any provider
page-open-source-app-organic-maps-descri: Offline navigation on OpenStreetMap data, with no location tracking
page-open-source-app-vlc-description: Plays almost any audio or video file, with no ads or accounts
page-open-source-app-grapheneos-descript: A hardened Android build for Pixel phones, with no Google services
page-open-source-app-debian-description: A community-run Linux distribution that many others are built on
page-open-source-app-ubuntu-description: A beginner-friendly Linux desktop with long-term support releases
page-open-source-app-home-assistant-desc: Runs your smart home locally, without the vendor's cloud
page-open-source-app-immich-description: A self-hosted photo and video library on hardware you own
page-open-source-app-logseq-description: Notes and journals stored as plain files on your device
page-open-source-app-libreoffice-descrip: Documents, spreadsheets, and slides that open the files you already have
page-open-source-app-localsend-descripti: Sends files between devices over your own network
page-open-source-app-obs-description: Records and streams your screen, with no watermarks or subscriptions
page-open-source-app-blender-description: A full 3D suite, from modeling and animation to video editing
page-open-source-app-inkscape-descriptio: Vector drawing for logos, icons, and illustration
page-open-source-app-gimp-description: A long-standing image editor for photo retouching and design work
page-open-source-alternativeto-descripti: Discover powerful open-source alternatives to popular software.
page-open-source-ai-intro: AI cuts both ways here. The AI assistants most people use are proprietary services running on someone else's computer. But they are also, right now, one of the best tools available to help you get started with open source software. There are also open AI models you can run yourself that never send information back to a centralized AI provider.
page-open-source-ai-assist-title: AI prompts to help you get started
page-open-source-ai-assist-description-1: The hard part of switching is rarely the software itself: it is knowing what exists, whether it is any good, and what to do when something breaks. An AI assistant closes most of that gap, and it can read a project's code and answer in plain words, so you do not need a developer's skill set to check the one thing that worries you.
page-open-source-ai-prompts-lead: Things worth asking. Click any card to copy it, then fill in the blanks:
page-open-source-ai-prompt-alternatives-: What are the open source alternatives to [app] for [my device], and what would I give up by switching?
page-open-source-ai-prompt-install-text: Walk me through installing [app] on [my system], one step at a time, and tell me what each step does.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-error-text: I tried [this] and got [this error]. What does it mean, and what should I try next?
page-open-source-ai-prompt-reputation-te: Who makes [app]? How is it funded, is it still actively maintained, and has it ever had security problems?
page-open-source-ai-prompt-policy-text: Find [app]'s privacy policy and license, and tell me in plain language what data leaves my device.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-permissions-t: [App] is asking for permission to access my contacts. Check the project's source code and tell me what it actually does with them.
page-open-source-ai-tip-description: Add "always prefer free and open source options, and tell me the license" to your assistant's configuration and it becomes the default for every future conversation. Open alternatives then show up in the AI assistant's answers without you having to ask for them specifically.
page-open-source-local-ai-title: Running AI locally on your own computer
page-open-source-local-ai-description-1: Most chat assistants are services. Your prompt leaves your device, the company sets the rules, and access can be changed, priced, or discontinued at any time. It does not have to work that way.
page-open-source-local-ai-description-2: Models with published weights can be downloaded and run on hardware you already own. No account. No API key. No subscription. Nothing sent anywhere, so you can unplug the network and keep working. And once the file is on your disk, it is yours. No one can deprecate your local AI model, silently change it, or take it away. A model you download today will still answer questions on that machine in ten years.
page-open-source-local-ai-app-jan-descri: A desktop app with a visual model browser and no command line at any point. Built for offline use, with no mandatory cloud account.
page-open-source-local-ai-app-ollama-des: Downloads and chats with models entirely from its desktop app, and doubles as the engine behind a large ecosystem of other tools.
page-open-source-local-ai-app-lm-studio-: The most polished first install of the three, with a model browser that flags what your hardware can handle. The app itself is closed source, though the models it runs are not.
page-open-source-local-ai-note-title: What does it mean for an AI model to be "open"?
page-open-source-local-ai-note-descripti: Most AI models described as open publish their weights but not their training data or the code that produced them. You can run and adapt them; you cannot fully study or rebuild them. By the definitions set out on this page, that is closer to source-available than to free software.

It is still a large improvement on the closed alternative. An open-weight model you have downloaded runs without permission, cannot be revoked, keeps working when the company behind it changes direction or disappears, and can be independently tested by anyone who wants to check its behavior. Those are the same benefits, freedom to leave and software that outlives its maker, that the rest of this page is about. The Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition sets out what full openness would require, and a handful of models such as AI2's OLMo and EleutherAI's Pythia already meet it.
page-open-source-movement-description: Long before Ethereum existed, people were making these arguments and winning them. They wrote the licenses described on this page, won the court cases that made publishing code lawful, and built the tools millions rely on to speak and read unwatched. Privacy, ownership, repair, freedom of speech, the right to read: Ethereum holds the same commitments because it grew out of the same tradition, and the organizations below are where much of that ground is still defended, case by case and tool by tool. Much of what this page describes exists because of them. They are independent of Ethereum and set their own priorities, and all of them are worth supporting.
page-open-source-org-fsf-description: Maintains the free software definition and the GNU project
page-open-source-org-eff-description: Defends digital civil liberties in the courts and in public policy
page-open-source-org-osi-description: Stewards the open source definition and the list of approved licenses
page-open-source-org-tor-description: Builds open anonymity and anti-censorship tools
page-open-source-org-fight-for-the-futur: Campaigns for an open internet and against mass surveillance
page-open-source-org-internet-archive-de: Preserves the web and defends the right to read, lend, and archive online
page-open-source-movement-wider-descript: Some of the most useful knowledge ever put online is free because the people who built it chose to keep it that way, including peer-reviewed university textbooks, course material from world-class universities, encyclopedias in hundreds of languages, maps of the entire planet, or research that would otherwise sit behind a paywall.
page-open-source-resources-data: Open science: <doaj>DOAJ</doaj> for open access journals, <arxiv>arXiv</arxiv> for preprints, and <zenodo>Zenodo</zenodo> for research data and code.
page-open-source-resources-culture: Open culture: <cc>Creative Commons</cc>, the public domain, <wikipedia>Wikipedia</wikipedia>, <osm>OpenStreetMap</osm>.
page-open-source-ethereum-description-1: Ethereum is a public network built through open specifications and independently developed software. No single company owns the protocol or has exclusive control over how people access it. Anyone can inspect the code, review proposed changes, run software that connects to the network, or build applications that use the protocol.
page-open-source-ethereum-item-1: The network's rules are implemented by multiple independent teams, so no single company controls what it does.
page-open-source-ethereum-item-2: Anyone can run a node and independently verify the network.
page-open-source-ethereum-item-3: Researchers and developers discuss protocol changes openly.
page-open-source-ethereum-item-4: Contributors can improve code, documentation, translations, education, tooling, and community resources.
page-open-source-ethereum-description-2: A different future is possible, one where openness is built in and the things you rely on keep working for you.
page-open-source-ethereum-description-3: Ethereum's openness does not mean every application built on it is open source, safe, or trustworthy. You should still evaluate the software, contracts, teams, and risks involved. But the protocol itself is designed so that its foundations can be inspected and improved in public.
page-open-source-comparison-title: Proprietary, open source, and free software: what's the difference?
page-open-source-comparison-description: "Open" gets used loosely, and the differences matter. Four families cover almost everything you will meet:
page-open-source-comparison-proprietary-: You can use the software only under the vendor's terms. You generally cannot inspect, modify, or redistribute it.
No license to the source at all
page-open-source-comparison-source-avail: You can read the code. Commercial use, modification, or redistribution are restricted. Not open source.
BUSL 1.1, SSPL, many "open core" licenses. Not OSI-approved.
Terraform, which moved from the open MPL 2.0 to BUSL 1.1 in August 2023. That change is why the community forked OpenTofu.
page-open-source-comparison-permissive-r: You can generally use, study, modify, and share the software, including in commercial products, subject to license conditions.
page-open-source-comparison-permissive-e: Lighthouse, Reth, Besu, Teku (Apache 2.0); Nimbus (Apache 2.0 / MIT); this website (MIT)
page-open-source-comparison-copyleft-rig: You can use, study, modify, and share the software. If you distribute modified versions, the license may require you to pass on the same freedoms.
page-open-source-comparison-copyleft-exa: Linux (GPL-2.0); Ethereum clients: go-ethereum (GPL-3.0 for the binary, LGPL-3.0 for its libraries); Prysm, Nethermind, Grandine, Solidity (GPL-3.0)
page-open-source-copyleft-title: Ethereum runs on copyleft, not just on the word "open"
page-open-source-copyleft-description-1: Plenty of projects call themselves open. What matters is the license file, so here is ours.
page-open-source-copyleft-description-2: Ethereum's most critical infrastructure ships under the Free Software Foundation's own copyleft licenses: go-ethereum is GPL-3.0 with LGPL-3.0 libraries, and Prysm, Nethermind, Grandine, and the Solidity compiler are GPL-3.0, with Erigon under LGPL-3.0. Other clients take the permissive route: Lighthouse, Reth, Besu, and Teku are Apache 2.0.
page-open-source-copyleft-contribute: This website is MIT, and every change to this page is publicly visible. Anyone is free to <source>inspect the source code</source> or <issues>suggest changes</issues>.
page-open-source-copyleft-description-3: Client diversity is itself an application of the right to fork. No single implementation controls the network, and any of them can be replaced by something better without asking permission.
page-open-source-traditions-question: So is it "free software" or "open source"?
page-open-source-traditions-answer-1: "Free software" and "open source" come from related traditions. Free software emphasizes users' rights and freedom. Open source often emphasizes practical benefits such as collaboration, reliability, and better software. In practice, both describe software whose license grants people real rights to use, study, modify, and share it.
page-open-source-traditions-answer-2: This page uses the terms together, as FLOSS, because the distinction rarely changes what you can do with the software in front of you.
page-open-source-security-question: Isn't open source less secure if anyone can read the code?
page-open-source-security-answer-1: It is a fair question, and the answer is not a flat no. Publishing code does let attackers study it. But it lets everyone else study it too, and secrecy has a poor record as a defense: closed software has the same flaws, found later, disclosed on the vendor's schedule, and fixed when it suits them.
page-open-source-security-answer-2: The honest version is that openness is necessary but not sufficient. Serious bugs have sat unnoticed in widely used open projects for years, usually because critical infrastructure was being maintained by one or two unpaid people. What openness guarantees is that anyone can look and anyone can fix it; whether enough people do depends on how well the project is funded and staffed. That is worth checking before you depend on something, and it is an easy thing to ask about.
